One-line judgment: cement masons and concrete finishers do not just pour concrete and spread it flat; they turn fresh concrete into a formed surface that meets requirements for elevation, slope and surface quality and can be cured and repaired — checking, setting and aligning forms, signalling tanker drivers and controlling the discharge chute, organising the pour and directing spreading and consolidation, using screeds, trowels and power trowels to level, compact and finish, forming control joints, edges and trowelled or broomed surfaces, monitoring curing against wind, temperature and cold, applying hardening, sealing and waterproofing and repairs, and chipping out, levelling and pointing defects. O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), with an interest code of RC (Realistic, Conventional), and this occupation page does not mark Bright Outlook. The core boundary is that this occupation usually is not a uniformly licensed one, but crystalline silica, dust and skin contact protection, fall, excavation and machinery protection, equipment and energy isolation, personal protective equipment and inspection and stop-work authority are required separately under the jurisdiction and institutional rules; the conclusions on elevation, flatness, slope and curing of the formed surface are determined by the supervisor, the main contractor and authorised personnel according to the design documents and specifications, and are not decided by the operator alone.

Signals to keep exploring: you can keep wearing protection and maintain your work rhythm outdoors in weather, noise and dust, and are willing to complete each step in sequence within the time window before the concrete initially sets (the O*NET work context shows 96% continuously handle and control objects and tools by hand, 82% stand continuously or almost continuously, 84% work outdoors exposed to all weather conditions every day, 55% are exposed to contaminants every day (including cement dust and alkaline materials), 63% perform repetitive motions continuously, 70% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 86% wear common protective or safety equipment every day and 59% consider the pace determined by equipment speed extremely important), you can stop and report first rather than forcing a pour when forms are not aligned, the weather changes suddenly or equipment fails, and you are willing to write the pour, curing, inspection and stop-work records clearly and hand them over.

Conditions for pausing high investment first: you have not yet completed a full closed-loop exercise that runs from form checking and alignment, pouring, spreading and consolidation, levelling and finishing, control joints and edge treatment, to curing and defect repair; or you are unwilling to comply with dust and skin contact protection and personal protective equipment requirements, unwilling to work to procedure on equipment and energy isolation and fall protection, unwilling to stop and escalate when the weather or materials are abnormal and instead force the work; and do not treat having helped a family member finish a small patch of floor as proof that you already have the ability to control elevation, flatness and slope on a large formed surface and to cure and repair it.

Education, qualifications and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and the education survey shows 52% of respondents think less than a high school diploma is enough, 35% think a high school diploma or equivalent is needed and 13% think a postsecondary education certificate is needed; the occupation page lists 23 certifications (including Commercial/Industrial Flatwork Specialist - Surface Treatments, Aggregate Base Testing Technician, Shotcrete Nozzleman (Dry-Mix Process) and Concrete Strength Testing Technician from the American Concrete Institute International, Reinforced Concrete Special Inspector from the International Code Council, Concrete Finisher Assessment and Concrete Construction from the National Center for Construction Education and Research, and Concrete Slab Moisture Testing Technician from the International Concrete Repair Institute), and lists 3 position titles approved by the U.S. Department of Labor for registered apprenticeship (Cement Mason and Cement Mason Concrete Finisher, among others). In the United States, this occupation usually does not require a unified licence, but some states and projects have separate qualification requirements for concrete inspection and special work; in Chinese mainland, the related duties may fall within masonry, plastering and concrete work positions under a broader occupational framing, and work involving dust, noise, heat, confined spaces, temporary electrical work and machinery is subject to public rules on work safety and occupational health. Education and training, industry certification and apprenticeship experience, statutory qualification and practice eligibility, job hiring and authorization, and authority over formed-surface acceptance and stop-work decisions are five different things.

One line: this is a position that turns whether this slab of concrete was poured correctly, finished flat, jointed correctly and cured properly into reviewable evidence, producing form check and alignment records, pour, spread, consolidation and equipment use records, levelling, finishing, control joint and edge treatment records, self-check and review records for flatness, slope and elevation, curing, surface treatment and defect repair records, and weather, stop-work and handover records; it is not a structural design or mix design decision role, and it does not replace the determination of structural safety, formed-surface acceptance and stop/resume work by design, supervision and the main contractor. U.S. wages and employment use a public statistical framing, and this route obtained no occupational-level statistical framing for Chinese mainland, so this page shows the gap rather than filling in a proxy figure.

The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, pour preparation and pouring (checking that forms are correctly constructed, setting and aligning forms to the specified slope and depth, signalling tanker drivers and moving the chute, directing the pour and supervising spreading, operating vibrators to consolidate, and installing embedded items such as anchor bolts, plates and thresholds); second, surface finishing and forming (spreading and levelling with rakes, shovels, hand or power trowels and screeds, forming expansion joints and edges with edgers, jointers and straightedges, obtaining the specified finish by brooming, trowelling or grinding, and applying hardening, sealing and waterproofing materials); third, curing, repair and inspection (monitoring the effect of wind and heat or cold on curing, chipping, scraping and grinding high spots, cutting out damaged areas and drilling holes for and positioning reinforcing bars, grouting holes and cracks and levelling them, and cleaning, judging surface condition, recording and handing over). All three share one chain built around correct forms and elevation, dense spreading and consolidation, correct surface flatness and slope and joints, and traceable curing and repair.
Pour preparation and pouring

Check that the formwork is sound and sealed, set and align forms and elevation to the specified slope and depth → signal the tanker driver and move the discharge chute → organise the pour and supervise spreading and layering → operate the vibrator to consolidate and avoid segregation and missed vibration → install embedded items such as anchor bolts, plates and thresholds → produce pour and equipment use records
Surface finishing and forming

Level, float, trowel and finish are organised as separate steps with different working conditions and are not all completed within one uniform window before initial set; NRMCA CIP14 distinguishes preliminary levelling from later floating/trowelling: the later finishing waits until bleeding has stopped and there is no water sheen on the surface, and the timing is judged from the concrete and the environment; do not compress pouring through curing into one uniform window before initial set and do not speed up finishing by adding water or dry cement. Joints and curing follow the design and the actual process, and technical guidance does not replace statutory specifications or project plans. Complete the specified edges/joints, curing, and self-check of flatness, slope and elevation, and record them.

Schedule curing according to wind, temperature and cold effects and cover and sprinkle in good time → check flatness, slope and elevation against the design documents → record defects with location and cause and decide the repair method → chip out, clean, grout and level and re-check → escalate structural or mix design issues beyond your authority to authorised personnel → complete the curing period and handover records

Cement masons and concrete finishers centre on pouring, spreading, surface forming and curing of fresh concrete; brickmasons and blockmasons specialise in laying units and mortar, stonemasons in working and installing natural stone, plasterers and stucco masons in plastering and stucco finishes on walls and ceilings, terrazzo workers and finishers in terrazzo surfaces and finishing, reinforcing iron and rebar workers in cutting, tying and positioning reinforcement, and construction labourers in site assistance, material handling, cleaning and supporting the trades. Similar names or being on the same concrete and masonry site does not mean that material processes, work qualifications, acceptance or stop/resume work authority can be exchanged.
Core purpose

Make fresh concrete meet the design requirements for elevation, slope, flatness, surface quality and curing: verify forms and elevation so the formed surface is in the right position, use pour, consolidation and finishing records so the process is traceable, and use curing, defect repair and handover so problems are not carried into the subsequent structural and finishing trades.
Main objects and basis

The objects are fresh concrete and grout and slurry made from cement, sand and water, forms, moulds, expansion joints and edge components, embedded items such as anchor bolts, plates and thresholds, hardening, sealing, waterproofing and repair materials, and tools and equipment such as rakes, shovels, trowels, screeds, power trowels, vibrators, saws and pneumatic breakers; the people you work with include design, supervision, main contractor and project management personnel, tanker drivers and pumping and transport personnel, rebar, formwork, mechanical and electrical and other following trades, and material suppliers. The basis is the elevation, slope, flatness and expansion joint positions specified in the design documents and construction plan, the concrete material and mix and initial set and curing requirements, the weather, wind and temperature conditions, and the statutory requirements and institutional procedures for crystalline silica, dust, noise and skin contact protection and for fall, machinery and temporary electrical protection.
Core process

Checking and aligning forms, organising the pour and spreading, consolidation and embedded item installation, levelling, finishing and trowelling, forming expansion joints and edges, applying finishes and surface treatments, monitoring curing conditions and covering and sprinkling, re-checking flatness, slope and elevation, chipping, repair and cleaning, and recording and handover.
Main outputs

Form check, alignment and elevation records, pour, spread, consolidation and equipment use records, embedded item installation and position re-check records, levelling, finishing, finish and expansion joint and edge treatment records, flatness, slope and elevation self-check and review records, curing, covering and sprinkling records, defect, repair and cleaning records, and weather, stop-work and handover records.
Responsible party

You carry out formwork, pouring, finishing and curing and process self-checks according to the plan; design, materials, testing, project technical and quality management and acceptance responsibilities are allocated under the applicable project rules, and not all formed-surface self-checks are excluded from this occupation, nor is the same approval chain specified for all projects. Articles 28/30/55/57—59 of China's Work Safety Law: safety training and special operation qualifications are separate, procedures must be followed and hazards reported; where an emergency directly endangering personal safety is found, the worker has the right to stop their own work or, in accordance with the law, to take emergency measures and then evacuate, without first obtaining institutional stop-work authorization. Overall project stop/resume work and project acceptance are handled separately under the applicable rules and responsibilities. Articles 24/25/27/32/36—37 of the Regulations on the Administration of Construction Project Work Safety set out general and subcontractor responsibility, list special operations, technical briefing, protection and emergency evacuation, and training, and do not describe all cutting and vibrating operations as special operations.
Access and licensing

Overall project stop/resume work and project acceptance are handled separately under the applicable rules and responsibilities. Articles 24/25/27/32/36—37 of the Regulations on the Administration of Construction Project Work Safety set out general and subcontractor responsibility, list special operations, technical briefing, protection and emergency evacuation, and training, and do not describe all cutting and vibrating operations as special operations. For U.S. construction silica dust, check OSHA1926.1153: employers implement engineering/work-practice/respiratory controls according to Table1 for the specific equipment, indoors or outdoors and shift length, or handle it through the paragraph (d) exposure assessment route; wet methods and dust collection are not freely interchangeable, and respiratory protection and medical surveillance have applicable conditions. The O*NET 55% exposure to contaminants is not a silica dust measurement, an accident rate or evidence of compliance. For U.S. concrete construction equipment, check 1926.702: hand-guided powered trowels must have a control that cuts off power automatically when the operator releases the handle; for maintenance and servicing that could start unexpectedly and injure someone, all potentially hazardous energy must be locked out and tagged out. Other equipment and cleaning tasks are confirmed under the applicable rules, the manual and the hazardous energy plan, and the industrial 1910 clauses are not applied unconditionally to construction. Statutory conditions and the actual project position's authority are confirmed separately, and training and written authorization cannot replace statutory qualification; U.S. state-by-state contracting and inspection licensing was not checked this round.
Boundary of the conclusion

Process records support tracing the location, elevation and slope, materials, weather and period, and do not automatically form conclusions on structural safety, mix design or final project acceptance. Formal acceptance and project resumption are handled by the corresponding responsible parties under the actual project rules; your right to stop work and evacuate in the face of an immediate danger to persons is not excluded by that division.

Before starting work, check at least six items: the job duties (whether they lean toward large-area pouring and finishing, kerbs, footpaths and gutters, repair and chipping and patching, terrazzo and decorative surfaces, or inspection and testing support), whether you carry responsibility for directing the pour and coordinating tankers, pumping and pour pace, the working conditions (outdoors, season, night, heat or cold) and programme, whether crystalline silica and chemical materials are involved and the related training and protection requirements, who provides equipment, tools and protective equipment and their inspection and maintenance responsibility, and the pay method (hourly, by volume or by square metre) together with how quality and rework responsibility is divided.
Occupational framing

O*NET-SOC 47-2051.00 (SOC 47-2051, cement masons and concrete finishers within the construction and extraction major group), listed as Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and this occupation page does not mark Bright Outlook; the interest code is RC (Realistic 100, Conventional 38), and the specific interest areas corresponding to Realistic are led by physical and manual labour (93), building and carpentry (23), engineering (20) and transportation and machinery operation (19); the O*NET industry distribution shows 93% of this occupation in construction and 7% in other industries. The official U.S. scope of 47-2051.00 is to level and finish surfaces of poured concrete floors, walkways, pavements, roads, kerbs and similar surfaces using a variety of hand and power tools, and to align forms for footpaths, kerbs and gutters, patch holes and cut expansion joints with saws. The 2022 edition of China's occupational classification code explicitly lists concrete workers as 6-29-01-03 (PDF physical page 535), with tasks covering batching and mixing, pumping and pouring, forming and formwork, curing and repair and equipment maintenance. This overlaps with U.S. 47-2051, but the Chinese scope includes production and conveying, and no complete task-by-task statistical mapping has been established, so the name cannot be used to infer equivalent wages or qualifications.
Education and training path

BLS SOC47-2051 gives a typical entry of no formal educational credential, no related work experience and moderate-term on-the-job training; O*NET Job Zone1—2 is a level-level general preparation description, and 52%/35%/13% are respondents' judgments about the education new hires need, not the educational attainment of incumbents. The certification directory lists 23 items, and the apprenticeship field on the detail page lists 3 approved position titles (including aliases and existing names), which does not mean 3 separate open programmes or that all positions must hold every certification. The specific certification enrollment, fees and maintenance conditions must be checked with the body in each case. No sample of Chinese job posting education requirements and specific process training was obtained, so this is checked against the target position and no uniform junior or senior high school threshold is given.
Methods and tools

The O*NET detail page lists 4 software categories: accounting, analytical/scientific, information retrieval and project management; the Hot recruitment page shows 0 items (Lightcast2025 U.S. national job postings). 0 items refers to that recruitment table, not to the occupation having no software skills, and the number of categories is not a measured adoption rate or a uniform personal threshold. On site the main items are trowels, screeds, power trowels, vibrators, saws and chisels, measuring tools and formwork tools; PPE is selected according to the hazard assessment and the task, and an ordinary dust mask cannot replace the required certified respirator.
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly outdoor and on-site physical work. Pay and working hours

OOH notes that the masonry workers group is mostly full-time, may work overtime and has schedules affected by weather; the O*NET figures for this occupation of 52% facing time pressure every day, 78% with irregular schedules and 50% not automated at all are context distributions, not AI adoption rates. Precise BLS SOC47-2051: employment was 204,800 in 2025 and is projected to be 208,100 in 2035, a net increase of 3,300, or 1.6% growth, with about 13,600 openings per year on average over 2025—2035, and the self-employed share was 1.5% in 2025. OOH rounds the growth to 2%; openings include growth and replacement demand such as transfers out and exits, and are not 13600 new additions each year or a dedicated AI projection. The 2025 U.S. annual median is 57020 USD and the hourly median is 27.41, which is not starting pay. National Bureau of Statistics 2025 average annual wages for construction: 92,036 CNY for non-private units and 66,275 CNY for private units (pre-tax); this is all-position urban unit industry background, not the national wage, starting pay or upper and lower limits for concrete workers or for this U.S. occupation, and is not converted into an occupational monthly wage. Compare actual hours, pay method and seasonal stoppages, equipment protection and rework responsibility.

Cement masons and concrete finishers (O*NET-SOC 47-2051.00, Cement Masons and Concrete Finishers) use a variety of hand and power tools to level and finish surfaces of poured concrete such as floors, walks, footpaths, roads and kerbs; align forms for footpaths, kerbs and gutters; patch voids; and use saws to cut expansion joints. Daily work includes: checking that the forms used to hold the concrete are correctly constructed; setting and aligning forms to the required slope and depth; spreading, levelling and finishing concrete using rakes, shovels, hand or power trowels, hand or power screeds and trowelling tools; monitoring the effect of wind and heat or cold on curing throughout; forming expansion joints and edges using edgers, jointers and straightedges; signalling tanker drivers to adjust their position for pouring and moving the discharge chute to direct the flow of concrete; directly directing the pour and supervising labourers spreading with shovels or special tools; brooming concrete surfaces to produce a rough finish; applying hardening and sealing materials to the surface to promote curing and to waterproof or restore the surface; operating power vibrators to consolidate the concrete; installing anchor bolts, plates, thresholds and other embedded items in fresh concrete or patterns; wetting the surface for bonding and filling holes and cracks with grout or slurry and levelling them; waterproofing or repairing concrete surfaces with the appropriate materials; mixing cement, sand and water into concrete, grout or slurry using hoes, trowels, tampers and scrapers; chipping, scraping and grinding high spots, ridges and rough protrusions with pneumatic breakers and similar tools to repair the concrete; cutting out damaged areas and drilling holes for and positioning reinforcing bars to patch the concrete; wetting the concrete surface and grinding it with a rubbing stone to obtain the specified finish; cleaning chipped areas with a wire brush and judging by feel and observation whether the surface is rough or uneven; and making wooden forms and clamping moulds to the area to be repaired with hand tools. It carries responsibility for executing the process, surface quality and work safety and records, but does not replace the determination of structural safety, mix design, formed-surface acceptance and stop/resume work by design, supervision and the main contractor.

paragraphs: This page compares cement masons and concrete finishers with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. The adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean that position titles or work qualifications and acceptance and stop/resume work authority can be exchanged.

Evidence note: occupational directions and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 47-2051.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. framing); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are terrazzo workers and finishers, plasterers and stucco masons, and brickmasons, blockmasons and stonemasons (combined occupation), while stonemasons, reinforcing iron and rebar workers and construction labourers are same-chain directions among the O*NET related occupations; work qualifications and inspection and stop-work authority, and material, mix and acceptance determinations must be verified separately under each jurisdiction and institution and contract; this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares how cement masons and concrete finishers and the adjacent directions differ in duties and outputs; the basis for judgment is the main outputs, the object of responsibility and the qualifications and authorization required, not how similar the position titles are.

Brickmasons and blockmasons specialise in laying units and mortar, and their objects are discrete units and masonry; this occupation produces the pouring, spreading, surface forming and curing of fresh concrete, and the two differ in material state and process window.

If you would rather do unit masonry and mortar joints and vertical and level control, look first at brickmasons and blockmasons; if you would rather complete pouring, finishing and curing within the time window of fresh concrete, look first at this occupation.
Building walls and structures with brick, block and mortar, with outputs centring on masonry and mortar joint quality and verticality and levelness.
Brickmasons and blockmasons

Stonemasons specialise in cutting, carving and dry or wet fixing natural stone, and the material is stone; this occupation handles plastic fresh concrete and forms the surface within the initial set window.

If you would rather work with natural stone and do fabrication and installation, look first at stonemasons; if you would rather do concrete pouring and surface finishing, look first at this occupation.
Fabricating and installing natural stone components and finishes, with outputs centring on stone dimensions, joints and secure installation.
Stonemasons

Plasterers and stucco masons specialise in mortar and stucco finishes on walls and ceilings, working on walls and ceilings and mostly in vertical orientations; this occupation works concrete on horizontal or formed surfaces and has to control elevation, slope and expansion joints.

If you would rather do wall plastering and finish levelling, look first at plasterers and stucco masons; if you would rather do formed concrete surfaces and expansion joints and curing, look first at this occupation.
Applying plaster and stucco finishes and levelling on walls and ceilings, with outputs centring on wall flatness and finish quality.
Plasterers and stucco masons

Terrazzo workers and finishers specialise in terrazzo mixes, divider strips and grinding and polishing, and their process is closer to decorative surfacing; this occupation centres on large-area concrete pouring, finishing, curing and structurally related forming.

If you would rather do decorative surfacing and terrazzo work, look first at terrazzo workers and finishers; if you would rather do concrete pour organisation and surface finishing, look first at this occupation.
Making and finishing terrazzo surfaces and grinding, polishing and setting divider strips, with outputs centring on surface pattern and gloss.
Terrazzo workers and finishers

Reinforcing iron and rebar workers specialise in cutting, tying and positioning reinforcement, a structural step before pouring; this occupation organises the pour after reinforcement and formwork have passed inspection and is responsible for the formed surface quality.

If you would rather do reinforcement cutting, tying and positioning, look first at reinforcing iron and rebar workers; if you would rather do pour organisation and surface forming and curing, look first at this occupation.
Cutting, tying and positioning reinforcement to drawings, with outputs centring on bar size and spacing, cover and tying quality.
Reinforcing iron and rebar workers

Construction labourers specialise in site assistance, handling, cleaning and support and usually do not independently carry responsibility for pour organisation and formed surface quality; this occupation carries responsibility for form alignment, directing the pour, finishing and curing and its own process records.

If you would rather do site support, handling and cleaning, look first at construction labourers; if you would rather carry responsibility for pouring and formed surface quality, look first at this occupation.
Carrying out material handling, trade assistance, cleaning and support on the construction site, with outputs centring on site support and site condition.
Construction labourers

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main outputs, the object of responsibility and the qualifications and authorization required, not how similar the names are; once a direction is chosen, check item by item the target position's work surfaces and process steps, whether it carries responsibility for directing the pour and coordinating curing and acceptance, the working conditions (outdoors, season, night) and programme, and whether crystalline silica and chemical materials are involved and the related training and protection requirements, and keep written confirmation.

First complete a closed loop with self-made materials: given a fictional formwork and elevation note and a fictional set of weather and material conditions, write out form checking and alignment, the pour sequence and vibrator point layout, the process and timing for levelling, finishing, control joints and edge treatment, and curing and defect determination and repair methods, mark three possible quality or safety risks and two situations where work must stop, then ask a peer to challenge it; at the same time check whether the target position involves crystalline silica and chemical materials and the related training and protection requirements.
Working cement masons and concrete finishers

Use tools for reviewable steps such as drafting process plans and crew rotas, estimating material quantities and volumes, and organizing curing records, checklists and defect lists; the actual condition of forms, the actual weather and materials, the actual feel and appearance when finishing and trowelling, the actual positions of control joints, edges and slopes, and the defect repair method must still be checked and documented by you on site.
On-site construction and quality management positions

Before introducing automated pouring equipment, vibrating or finishing robots or automatic curing monitoring, first make clear the version of the design documents and elevation and slope data, equipment and energy isolation and protection measures, who handles anomalies and shutdowns, and who is responsible for formed surface quality and rework and acceptance conclusions, and ensure there is substantive human review and documentation before pouring and delivery.
Mentoring and skills training

Focus training on form checking and elevation and slope control, pour organisation and spreading and consolidation, levelling, finishing, trowelling and the specified finish, control joint and edge forming, the effect of wind and temperature on curing and covering and sprinkling, defect determination and repair, and dust control and skin and respiratory protection for crystalline silica, cement and chemical materials; also train the habit of staying cautious about automated equipment and automatic monitoring results and going back to on-site measurement and specification checks.

Conclusion: reviewable steps such as drafting process plans and rotas, estimating volumes and quantities, and organizing curing records, checklists and defect lists can be assisted by tools, but there is no official evidence that this replaces measuring forms and elevation on site, the actual operations of pouring, consolidating and finishing, on-site judgment of control joints, slope and surface quality, and responsibility for work safety and stop-work. Learn the basics and the rules first: form checking and elevation and slope control, pour organisation and spreading and consolidation, levelling, finishing, trowelling and the specified finish, control joint and edge forming, curing and defect determination and repair, and the rules for crystalline silica, dust, fall, machinery and temporary electrical protection and stopping and escalating; build the process and safety boundaries first, then learn equipment and automation assistance, and expand duties gradually according to job authorization.

The following five items are suggested editorial steps for deployment and review, confirmed against the project hazard assessment and rules; they are not a uniform five-step procedure or a construction release permit.

First confirm the processes and equipment you may take on independently, the design documents and elevation and slope version you rely on, whether the weather and material conditions meet the pouring requirements, and which matters must stop work and be escalated to authorised personnel.

Trial drafting, estimating and recording tools on permitted, reviewable steps; the control and review of automated equipment and monitoring follows the project's actual applicable requirements, and no uniform human one-by-one release is inferred from these suggestions.

Review the measured forms, elevation and slope, the actual material consistency and initial set, and the weather and temperature changes item by item, and judge whether the automatic results match the actual situation; where they do not, on-site measurements and the specifications take precedence and the work is redone.

Keep form check, alignment and elevation records, pour, spread and consolidation records, levelling, finishing, finish and control joint and edge treatment records and curing and repair records so the process is traceable.

Design, materials, quality and acceptance are borne by the corresponding parties under the actual contract and applicable specifications; you carry out self-checks and reporting as required. Articles 28/30/55/57—59 of China's Work Safety Law: safety training and special operation qualifications are separate, procedures must be followed and hazards reported; where an emergency directly endangering personal safety is found, the worker has the right to stop their own work or, in accordance with the law, to take emergency measures and then evacuate, without first obtaining institutional stop-work authorization. Overall project stop/resume work and project acceptance are handled separately under the applicable rules and responsibilities. Articles 24/25/27/32/36—37 of the Regulations on the Administration of Construction Project Work Safety set out general and subcontractor responsibility, list special operations, technical briefing, protection and emergency evacuation, and training, and do not describe all cutting and vibrating operations as special operations.

Organising the pour only on an automatic schedule or automatic monitoring results without checking the forms, elevation and actual materials causes elevation and slope deviations, surface defects, rework and structural risks (70% consider precision or accuracy extremely important; 44% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 11% very serious).

Use the design documents, on-site measurements and actual materials to verify automatic results, and where there is an inconsistency re-check the facts before updating the record; where structure or acceptance is involved, the basis and the limits must be stated.
Contact with crystalline silica dust, cement and chemical materials, and mishandling construction imagery and project documents, cause occupational health and compliance consequences.

For U.S. construction silica dust, check OSHA1926.1153: employers implement engineering, work practice or respiratory controls according to Table1 for the specific equipment, indoors or outdoors and shift length, or handle it through the paragraph (d) exposure assessment route; wet methods and dust collection are not freely interchangeable, and respiratory protection and medical surveillance have applicable conditions. The O*NET 55% exposure to contaminants is not a silica dust measurement, an accident rate or evidence of compliance. For U.S. concrete construction equipment, check 1926.702: hand-guided powered trowels must have a control that cuts off power automatically when the operator releases the handle; for maintenance and servicing that could start unexpectedly and injure someone, all potentially hazardous energy must be locked out and tagged out. Other equipment and cleaning tasks are confirmed under the applicable rules, the manual and the hazardous energy plan, and the industrial 1910 clauses are not applied unconditionally to construction. Project imagery and documents must first be checked for lawful purpose, confidentiality and permission, and must not be provided to unapproved tools.
Scheduling curing only on automatic results without looking at the actual wind, temperature and sunlight misses surface moisture loss, early cracking and frost damage risks.

Check the curing arrangements against three kinds of primary information — on-site temperature, wind and the actual concrete condition — and record and escalate discrepancies, noting the reason and time for any change.

Errors in elevation, slope and thickness conversion and deviations in control joint position and spacing cause poor drainage, uneven surfaces and rework (70% consider precision or accuracy extremely important; 63% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others).

Use the design documents, measuring tools and levels to check elevation, slope and joint positions, and double-check before pouring and saw cutting; deviations must be recorded and escalated, and incorrect positions must not be carried into pouring and saw cutting.
Handing the pour release, acceptance support and stop-work judgment to tools or unauthorized people creates a responsibility vacuum and makes it untraceable.

Take on only the processes for which you already have qualifications, training and a project assignment, and report hazards promptly; in an emergency directly endangering personal safety, stop your own work or evacuate in accordance with the law. Overall resumption and acceptance are not authorized by tools or the simulated materials on this page.

Temperature and humidity records and reminders can be assisted, while curing judgments are handled according to the actual control and review requirements. This is an editorial task analysis and does not prove that automation is impossible.

Chip, scrape and grind high spots and rough protrusions, cut out damaged areas and drill and locate reinforcement, and fill holes and cracks with grout or slurry and level them.

Defect lists and repair records can be assisted, while deciding how to handle them is done according to the actual control and review requirements. This is an editorial task analysis and does not prove that automation is impossible.
Be responsible for the completeness and reporting of process, material, equipment and safety inspection records.
Record the process, material batches, equipment use, safety inspections and stop-work situations, and report and file them as required.

Record templates and reminders can be assisted, while compliance judgments are handled according to the actual control and review requirements. This is an editorial task analysis and does not prove that automation is impossible.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and work responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of individuals or institutions; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, the material and mix notes, the construction organisation design and the institution's safety and occupational health management system and contract.

Dust and wet cement contact, falls and person-machine injuries, hazardous energy, repetitive physical work and out-of-scope acceptance are task risk analysis; specific controls follow the jurisdiction and the actual task. For U.S. construction silica dust, check OSHA1926.1153: employers implement engineering, work practice or respiratory controls according to Table1 for the specific equipment, indoors or outdoors and shift length, or handle it through the paragraph (d) exposure assessment route; wet methods and dust collection are not freely interchangeable, and respiratory protection and medical surveillance have applicable conditions. The O*NET 55% exposure to contaminants is not a silica dust measurement, an accident rate or evidence of compliance. For U.S. concrete construction equipment, check 1926.702: hand-guided powered trowels must have a control that cuts off power automatically when the operator releases the handle; for maintenance and servicing that could start unexpectedly and injure someone, all potentially hazardous energy must be locked out and tagged out. Other equipment and cleaning tasks are confirmed under the applicable rules, the manual and the hazardous energy plan, and the industrial 1910 clauses are not applied unconditionally to construction. Articles 28/30/55/57—59 of China's Work Safety Law: safety training and special operation qualifications are separate, procedures must be followed and hazards reported; where an emergency directly endangering personal safety is found, the worker has the right to stop their own work or, in accordance with the law, to take emergency measures and then evacuate, without first obtaining institutional stop-work authorization. Overall project stop/resume work and project acceptance are handled separately under the applicable rules and responsibilities. Articles 24/25/27/32/36—37 of the Regulations on the Administration of Construction Project Work Safety set out general and subcontractor responsibility, list special operations, technical briefing, protection and emergency evacuation, and training, and do not describe all cutting and vibrating operations as special operations.

entries.answer: Using a variety of hand and power tools to level and finish surfaces of poured concrete such as floors, walks, footpaths, roads and kerbs; aligning forms for footpaths, kerbs and gutters; patching voids; and using saws to cut control joints: checking that the forms used to hold the concrete are correctly constructed; setting and aligning forms to the required slope and depth; spreading, levelling and finishing concrete with rakes, shovels, hand or power trowels, screeds and trowelling tools; monitoring the effect of wind and heat or cold on curing throughout; forming control joints and edges with edgers, jointers and straightedges; signalling tanker drivers to adjust their position and moving the discharge chute; directly directing the pour and supervising labourers spreading with shovels or special tools; brooming a rough surface; applying hardening and sealing materials to cure and waterproof or restore the surface; operating a power vibrator to consolidate the concrete; installing anchor bolts, plates, thresholds and other embedded items; wetting the surface and filling holes and cracks with grout or slurry and levelling them; waterproofing or repairing the surface with the appropriate materials; mixing cement, sand and water with hoes, trowels, tampers and scrapers; chipping, scraping and grinding high spots and rough protrusions with pneumatic breakers and similar tools; cutting out damaged areas and drilling and locating reinforcement; wetting and grinding with a rubbing stone to obtain the specified finish; cleaning with a wire brush and judging surface condition by feel and observation; and making and clamping wooden forms for the area to be repaired.

entries.answer: The main risks include respiratory and skin exposure to crystalline silica dust and cement and chemical materials, falls from edges, excavations and heights and machinery and vehicle injuries, entanglement and crushing from failure to implement equipment and energy isolation, ergonomic injury from long periods of standing, bending, kneeling, repetitive motions and lifting, exposure from unsuitable or failed personal protective equipment, and quality and safety responsibility risks from confirming formed-surface acceptance and stop-work judgments beyond your authority; controls depend on confirming forms, work faces and safety conditions before work, wet methods, ventilation and protection for dust and chemical materials, fall, excavation, machinery and temporary electrical protection and equipment energy isolation and lockout/tagout, correct selection, inspection and replacement of personal protective equipment, and a clear stop-work and escalation path.

entries.answer: The fit signals are being able to complete pouring, levelling, finishing and curing in sequence within the initial set window, being able to check forms, elevation and slope clearly, being able to keep wearing protection outdoors and in dust and noise, and stopping and reporting first when forms are not aligned or the weather or equipment is abnormal; the key is whether you have reviewable form and elevation records, pouring, finishing and curing records, and defect and repair records, rather than only having helped a family member finish a small patch of floor or a piece of site experience.

entries.answer: Drafting process sequences and rotas, estimating volumes and material quantities, organizing curing and inspection records, and defect lists and progress and hours statistics can all be assisted; measuring forms and elevation, the actual operations of pour organisation, consolidation and finishing, judging control joints, slope and surface quality, and safety protection and stopping and escalating are still checked and owned by authorized personnel.

subject.name: Cement Masons and Concrete Finishers
subject.summary: This page entry corresponds to cement masons and concrete finishers (O*NET-SOC 47-2051.00, Cement Masons and Concrete Finishers): using a variety of hand and power tools to level and finish surfaces of poured concrete such as floors, walks, footpaths, roads and kerbs, and aligning forms for footpaths, kerbs and gutters, patching voids and cutting control joints with saws — checking, setting and aligning forms, signalling tanker drivers and controlling the discharge chute, organising the pour and directing spreading and consolidation, levelling and finishing with trowels, screeds and power trowels, forming control joints and edges and producing trowelled or broomed finishes to the design, monitoring the effect of wind and temperature on curing and applying hardening and sealing materials, and chipping, grouting and levelling to repair defects; the work is mainly outdoor and on-site physical work (96% continuously handle and control objects and tools by hand, 82% stand continuously or almost continuously, 84% work outdoors exposed to all weather conditions every day, 55% are exposed to contaminants every day, 70% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 86% wear common protective equipment every day), and its duties do not replace the determination of structural safety, formed-surface acceptance and stop/resume work by design, supervision and the main contractor; the occupation page does not mark Bright Outlook.
